overview.title: Greedy search and pluggable sampling functions
overview.main_topic: Why the mini-GPT repeats itself under greedy decoding, and refactoring compiled_generate() to accept a sampling strategy function.
overview.central_idea: Repetition is a natural consequence of next-token training plus always choosing the argmax (greedy search). The model actually outputs a full distribution over 32,000 tokens; by making the token-choice rule a parameter (sample_fn), we can explore that distribution, starting with greedy search as one such function and then random categorical sampling.
overview.importance: Decoding strategy is a separate design choice from the model. This page sets up the code structure used for every strategy in the section (greedy, random with temperature, top-K) and introduces the vocabulary of greedy search and sampling strategy.
learning_objectives: Explain why a next-token predictor trained on broad text falls back on common words and repeated patterns.
Define greedy search and state its weakness.
Describe the model's output at a generation step as a categorical distribution over the 32,000-token vocabulary.
Read the refactored compiled_generate(prompt, sample_fn, max_length=64) line by line.
Implement greedy search as a sampling function using ops.argmax.
State what keras.random.categorical() does with logits.
prerequisites: Logits and softmax (the 'What is a logit?' sidebar, p.501).
The repetition problem noted at the start of 16.2.4 (p.504).

summary:
The page continues 16.2.4 by diagnosing the repetition seen on p.503-504. The authors argue it is **not a bug but a consequence of the training objective**: the model predicts the most likely next token across roughly a billion words on many topics, and when there is no obvious continuation, guessing common words or repeated word patterns is an effective strategy that the model learns almost immediately. Stopped very early, it would emit "the" over and over, the most common English word.

The generation loop so far has always taken the most likely token, yet the model's output at each step is a **probability distribution over all 32,000 vocabulary tokens**. Taking the argmax each step is called **greedy search**: the simplest use of the predictions but not the only one. Adding randomness lets us explore the learned distribution more broadly and avoid getting stuck in loops of high-probability sequences.

To experiment, the authors refactor `compiled_generate()` to take a `sample_fn`, a function mapping the model's prediction vector (at the last real position) to the next token. They call this the **sampling strategy**. The loop is otherwise identical to listing 16.10: tokenize, pad to `max_length=64`, call `mini_gpt.predict()` on the fixed-shape input, read `prediction[0, i - 1]`, and now set `tokens[i]` from `sample_fn(prediction)`, converted to NumPy and to a Python int.

Greedy search becomes a one-liner, `ops.argmax(preds)`, passed as `compiled_generate(prompt, greedy_search)`. Finally the authors note that the Transformer's outputs define a **categorical distribution** per time step, which we could sample directly instead of taking the maximum: `keras.random.categorical()` applies a softmax to the predictions (logits) and draws a random sample. The code and its output follow on p.506.

paragraphs.excerpt: This isn’t so much a bug as it’s a direct consequence of our training objective.
paragraphs.what_it_says: Repetition comes from the training objective. Predicting the most likely next token across about a billion words on many topics, the model learns that when no continuation is obvious, guessing common words or repeated word patterns works well. It learns this almost immediately; stopped very early, it would generate "the" incessantly, the most common English word.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Cross-entropy training rewards putting probability mass where it is most often correct. When the context is uninformative, the best guess is the marginal (unconditional) frequency of tokens, hence "the". As the model improves, it learns that recently seen phrases are likely to recur (text does repeat itself), which, combined with argmax decoding, becomes a self-reinforcing loop.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It shifts attention from 'fix the model' to 'fix the decoding': a model can have learned a good distribution yet produce degenerate output when we only ever take its mode.
paragraphs.technical_idea: The very first thing a language model learns is roughly the unigram distribution; argmax of the unigram distribution is the single most frequent token.

terminology.meaning: Here: minimize cross-entropy of the next token given previous tokens (p(token | past tokens)).
(Not the book's term.) How often each token appears regardless of context.

p.488: chapter 15 summary defines a language model as learning p(token | past tokens).

paragraphs.excerpt: During our generative loop, we have always chosen the most likely predicted token
paragraphs.what_it_says: The loop has always picked the most likely token, but the model's output is a probability distribution over all 32,000 tokens of the vocabulary.
paragraphs.what_it_means: At each step mini_gpt produces a vector of 32,000 logits for the next position; listings 16.9-16.10 collapsed this rich object to a single index with argmax, discarding information about the other plausible continuations.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Recognizing the output as a distribution is what makes sampling strategies possible.

paragraphs.excerpt: Using the most likely output at each generation step is called greedy search.
paragraphs.what_it_says: Choosing the most likely output each step is greedy search: straightforward but not the only option. Adding randomness explores the learned distribution more broadly and can keep generation from getting stuck in loops of high-probability token sequences.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Greedy search is deterministic: the same prompt always gives the same text, and once the context makes a phrase likely, it is chosen again. Random choices let the generator leave such attractors.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This names the baseline every other strategy is compared against (random sampling on p.506, top-K on p.506-507).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Greedy search picks argmax p(x_t | x_<t) at each step; it does not even find the most probable overall sequence, since a locally best choice can lead to a globally worse one.

terminology.meaning: Decoding that always selects the most probable next token.

connections: p.530: chapter summary: greedy search, random sampling, top-K sampling.
p.508: beam search is mentioned as another strategy.

paragraphs.what_it_says: The generation function is refactored to take a function mapping model predictions to a next-token choice; this function is called the sampling strategy.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Separating 'how we compute the distribution' (the model) from 'how we pick from it' (sample_fn) lets us swap strategies without touching the loop.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It is a simple higher-order-function design that mirrors how real libraries expose samplers as interchangeable objects.

terminology.meaning: A rule (here, a Python function) that turns the prediction vector into the next token.

paragraphs.what_it_says: Greedy search can now be written as a simple function passed to compiled_generate().
paragraphs.what_it_means: The behaviour of listing 16.10 is recovered exactly by passing greedy_search; the refactor changes no results.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Checks that the new interface is a generalization of the old loop.

paragraphs.excerpt: The Transformer outputs define a categorical distribution where each token has a certain
paragraphs.what_it_says: The outputs define a categorical distribution with a probability per token at each step. Instead of taking the most likely token we can sample from it: keras.random.categorical() passes the predictions through softmax to get probabilities and then samples randomly.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Because mini_gpt outputs logits (no final softmax, p.501), they can be handed straight to keras.random.categorical, which interprets its input as unnormalized log-probabilities. A token with probability 0.3 will be chosen about 30% of the time.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is pure ancestral sampling from the model: the generated text is a genuine sample from the distribution the model learned, which brings diversity but also the risk of wandering off (shown on p.506).
paragraphs.technical_idea: categorical(logits) draws index i with probability softmax(logits)_i; it expects a 2-D input (batch, classes), which is why p.506 uses preds[None, :].

terminology.meaning: A distribution over a finite set of outcomes with probabilities summing to 1.
Keras op that samples class indices from logits.

concepts.name: Greedy search
concepts.definition: Selecting the most probable token at every generation step.
concepts.intuition: Always take the safest next word.
concepts.technical: x_t = argmax_i z_i where z are the logits; equivalent to argmax of softmax(z).
concepts.significance: Simple and deterministic, but leads to repetitive loops in the mini-GPT.
concepts.misconception: That greedy search finds the most probable sentence; it only optimizes each step locally.

concepts.name: Sampling strategy
concepts.definition: The rule that maps a model's predicted distribution to a chosen next token.
concepts.intuition: The model proposes; the sampling strategy decides.
concepts.technical: Implemented as sample_fn(prediction) -> token id; examples are greedy (argmax), random categorical sampling, temperature scaling, top-K.
concepts.significance: Changes output quality dramatically without retraining.
concepts.misconception: That generation quality depends only on the model.

concepts.name: Sampling from a categorical distribution
concepts.definition: Drawing a token at random with probability equal to its softmax probability.
concepts.intuition: Roll a weighted die with 32,000 faces.
concepts.technical: P(x_t = i) = exp(z_i) / Σ_j exp(z_j); keras.random.categorical(logits, num_samples).
concepts.significance: Lets the generator explore the learned distribution and escape repetition.
concepts.example: If 'the' has p = 0.4 and 'a' has p = 0.1, 'the' is sampled about four times as often as 'a'.
concepts.misconception: That keras.random.categorical expects probabilities; it expects logits and applies softmax itself.

concepts.name: Logits
concepts.definition: Unnormalized log probabilities output by the model's final projection.
concepts.intuition: Scores where bigger means more likely; softmax turns them into probabilities.
concepts.technical: p = softmax(z); argmax is unchanged by softmax since it is monotonic.
concepts.significance: Both greedy_search and random_sample operate directly on logits.
concepts.misconception: That you must apply softmax before argmax; it makes no difference to argmax.

math.title: Greedy search vs categorical sampling
math.source_text: In words: "Using the most likely output at each generation step is called greedy search" and "keras.random.categorical() will pass our predictions through a softmax function to get a probability distribution and then randomly sample it."

variables.meaning: logit vector at the last real position, prediction[0, i-1]
the token chosen for position t (tokens[i] in the code)

math.operations: Softmax normalizes exponentiated logits; greedy takes the index of the largest logit; sampling draws an index according to p.
math.purpose: Makes precise the two decoding rules contrasted on the page.
math.interpretation: Greedy uses only the mode of the distribution; sampling uses all of it.
math.intuition: Greedy always picks the tallest bar; sampling throws a dart whose landing chances are the bar heights.
math.numerical_example: Logits z = [2.0, 1.0, 0.1] over tokens ["the", "a", "my"]: e^z ≈ [7.389, 2.718, 1.105], sum ≈ 11.212, p ≈ [0.659, 0.242, 0.099]. Greedy always outputs "the"; sampling outputs "the" ≈66% of the time, "a" ≈24%, "my" ≈10%.

code.title: compiled_generate() with a pluggable sampling function
code.what_it_does: Generates text from a prompt up to 64 tokens, using a caller-supplied function to choose each next token from the model's logits.

line_explanations.explanation: New sample_fn parameter: the sampling strategy. max_length stays 64.
Tokenize the prompt with SentencePiece, convert to a Python list of ints, record its length.
Pad with zeros to exactly max_length so predict() always sees shape (1, 64) and the compiled function is reused (p.503).
Fill positions prompt_length .. 63 one at a time.
Run the full (padded) sequence through the compiled model; output shape (1, 64, 32000) logits.
Take the logits at position i - 1, which predict the token at position i. The causal mask guarantees the zero padding after position i - 1 does not influence them.
Apply the sampling strategy and convert the (possibly backend) tensor result to NumPy.
np.array(...).item() turns either a scalar (argmax) or a 1-element array (categorical sample) into a Python int stored in the token list.

code.inputs_outputs: Inputs: prompt string, sample_fn mapping a (32000,) logit vector to a token id, max_length. Output: detokenized string of 64 tokens.
code.algorithm: Autoregressive decoding with fixed-shape padded inputs and a pluggable token-selection rule.
code.theory_link: Separates the learned distribution p(x_t | x_<t) from the decision rule applied to it.

parameters.name: sample_fn

Pass the function itself (not its result) to the generator.

code.theory_link: Greedy search, the baseline named on this page.

deeper.title: Why 'the' first: the model learns the unigram distribution before context
deeper.body:
1. At initialization the logits are near-uniform, giving loss ≈ ln(32,000) ≈ 10.4.
2. The quickest way to reduce cross-entropy is to match overall token frequencies, ignoring context. This alone drops the loss substantially.
3. Under that unigram model, argmax is always the most frequent token, "the", so greedy decoding prints "the the the...", exactly what the authors predict for an early-stopped model.
4. With more training the model conditions on context, but where context is ambiguous it still hedges toward frequent words and recently used patterns. Greedy decoding turns that hedging into loops.

(Steps 1-2 are standard reasoning added here, not from the book.)

deeper.title: Analogy: a cautious improviser
deeper.body: An improviser who always says the single most predictable line ends up repeating catchphrases. One who picks lines at random, weighted by how sensible they are, sounds more natural but sometimes says something odd. The next pages tune between these extremes with temperature and top-K.

deeper.title: Greedy is not the most likely sequence
deeper.body: Suppose step 1 offers A (p = 0.6) or B (p = 0.4). After A the best next token has p = 0.3; after B one has p = 0.9. Greedy picks A then the 0.3 token: joint probability 0.18. Choosing B first gives 0.4 × 0.9 = 0.36. Greedy search is myopic; beam search (mentioned on p.508) partially addresses this by keeping several candidates. (Illustrative numbers.)

misconceptions.claim: Repetition means the model has a bug.
misconceptions.correction: The authors say it is a direct consequence of the next-token training objective combined with always choosing the most likely token.

misconceptions.claim: The model outputs a single predicted token.
misconceptions.correction: It outputs a probability distribution (as logits) over all 32,000 vocabulary tokens; choosing one is a separate step.

misconceptions.claim: Softmax must be applied before ops.argmax for greedy search.
misconceptions.correction: Softmax is monotonic, so argmax of logits equals argmax of probabilities.
It fixes the loops but explores too much (p.506), which motivates temperature and top-K.

takeaways: The mini-GPT repeats itself because next-token training favours common words and patterns, and greedy decoding always picks them.
An early-stopped model would print "the" endlessly, the most frequent English word.
The model's output is a distribution over 32,000 tokens; greedy search keeps only its argmax.
compiled_generate() now takes a sample_fn: the sampling strategy is a swappable function.
keras.random.categorical() softmaxes logits and samples, giving random sampling.

questions.question: According to the authors, why would a model stopped very early in training generate "the" incessantly?
options: Because "the" is the most common English word, and the model quickly learns to guess common words
Because of the padding with zeros
Because the causal mask hides all other tokens
questions.answer: Because "the" is the most common English word, and the model quickly learns to guess common words
questions.explanation: The page states exactly this. Token ids and padding are unrelated to which token is most probable; the causal mask hides future positions, not vocabulary entries.

questions.question: What is greedy search, and how is it implemented as a sample_fn?
questions.answer: Choosing the most likely token at each step; def greedy_search(preds): return ops.argmax(preds).
questions.explanation: Defined in the third printed paragraph and the second code block.

questions.question: Why does compiled_generate() read prediction[0, i - 1] rather than prediction[0, i]?
questions.answer: The output at position i - 1 is the model's prediction of the next token, i.e. the token at position i. Position i currently holds padding.
questions.explanation: A language model's output at each position predicts the following token (p.502); the causal mask ensures position i - 1's prediction ignores the zero padding after it.

questions.question: Logits for three candidate tokens are [2.0, 1.0, 0.1]. What does greedy search output, and with what probability does categorical sampling output the second token?
questions.answer: Greedy outputs the first token; the second is sampled with probability e^1 / (e^2 + e^1 + e^0.1) ≈ 0.242.

questions.question: What does keras.random.categorical() do with the predictions passed to it, per the book?
options: Passes them through softmax to get a probability distribution and samples it randomly
Normalizes them to sum to 1 and returns the probabilities
Keeps only the top K values
questions.answer: Passes them through softmax to get a probability distribution and samples it randomly
questions.explanation: Stated in the last paragraph. Argmax is greedy search; returning probabilities is just softmax; top-K is a later strategy (p.506-507).

questions.question: What is the design benefit of passing sample_fn into compiled_generate()?
questions.answer: It separates the model's distribution from the decision rule, so different strategies (greedy, random, temperature, top-K) can be tried without rewriting the loop, and the compiled predict() is reused for all.
questions.explanation: The authors introduce it explicitly to experiment with sampling strategies.

questions.question: Can you explain in your own words why adding randomness helps avoid loops of high-probability sequences, and what risk it introduces?
questions.answer: Randomness lets the generator pick a less likely but reasonable token that breaks the loop; the risk is picking unlikely, incoherent tokens, as p.506 shows.
questions.explanation: Self-check on the page's central argument.
